pages.x: After years of civil war and American bombing, the communist Khmer Rouge took Cambodia's capital, Phnom Penh, on 17 April 1975. Within days they drove its two million people into the countryside at gunpoint, even the sick from hospitals. They declared Year Zero: money, markets, schools and religion were abolished.

The movement was led by Saloth Sar, who called himself Pol Pot, a former teacher who had studied in Paris. He dreamed of a pure peasant nation that relied on nobody. Few Cambodians even knew his name; orders came from Angkar, the Organisation.

City people, the educated, monks, Vietnamese and Cham Muslims, even people who wore glasses, were singled out. Families were split up and worked in the fields from dawn to dark on a few spoonfuls of rice. Hundreds of thousands were executed and buried in mass graves, and many more died of hunger and disease.
pages.of: people died, about one in four

pages.x: In a former high school in Phnom Penh, the prison called S-21, at least 14,000 people were photographed, tortured into confessing and killed. Only a handful survived. Today it is the Tuol Sleng Genocide Museum, its walls covered with the prisoners' photographs.

After Khmer Rouge raids across its border, Vietnam invaded in December 1978 and took Phnom Penh in January 1979. Pol Pot fled to the jungle along the Thai border, where his forces fought on for years, backed by China and still holding Cambodia's seat at the United Nations.

Pol Pot died in 1998 without facing trial. A court set up with the United Nations later convicted a few of the surviving leaders of genocide and crimes against humanity. Cambodia has rebuilt, but almost every family lost someone, and the killing fields at Choeung Ek are now a memorial.
pts: About a quarter of Cambodians died
Ended by the Vietnamese invasion of 1979
